abstract.p: This study investigated the proteomic landscape of sound and carious coronal dentin to uncover the molecular signatures of host response, including tissue degradation, inflammation, and repair, across progressive stages of caries lesions. Dentin from de-identified human molars, grouped into six clusters of three teeth each, was pulverized to obtain ~ 1g of tissue per cluster (n=6). G1 and G2 protein extracts were obtained using guanidine before and after demineralization. Extracts from sound (S), distinct dentin caries (DDC), and extensive dentin caries (EDC) lesions were digested with trypsin and analyzed by label-free relative quantification via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Spectral data were matched against the UniProt Homo sapiens database using Mascot and Sequest HT in Proteome Discoverer. Statistical analysis using the limma package identified differentially expressed (DE) proteins (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05), and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) revealed key pathways, regulators, and networks. A total of 320 proteins were identified, with differential expression observed in 80 for EDC×S, 16 for EDC×DDC, and only 3 for DDC×S. In the G2×G1 comparison, 200 proteins exhibited differential recovery in at least one of the extracts. Proteins such as S100A8, S100A12, DEFA1, SERPINB1, MPO, and PRTN3 were up-regulated in EDC compared to DDC and S. TIMP-3, MMP20, DMP1, and other collagen and matrix-associated proteins showed higher coverage in G2 than in G1, revealing extract-specific profiles. Functional analysis highlighted enrichment in immune and inflammatory pathways, with strong activation of neutrophil degranulation, antimicrobial peptides, neutrophil extracellular trap signaling, and macrophage alternative activation in carious tissues. In conclusion, this study reveals stage-specific proteomic signatures in caries, reflecting a dynamic interplay between microbial-induced degradation and host-driven defense and repair. These findings offer new molecular insights into caries pathophysiology and may inform future diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Dental caries remains the most prevalent chronic disease worldwide, disproportionately affecting children and older adults (Peres et al. 2019). Although caries is a multifactorial condition shaped by biological, behavioral, and environmental factors (Selwitz et al. 2007), the molecular mechanisms underlying the dentin-pulp complex’s response to bacterial invasion are not fully understood. A central question in cariology is the extent to which tissue destruction, particularly in lesions extending into dentin, is driven by bacterial activity versus host-mediated responses (Peled et al. 2023). To address this, it is essential to view caries as a tissue-specific disease, where shifts in microbial diversity and function can trigger host responses (Simon-Soro et al. 2013). While recent studies have highlighted the microbial and enzymatic contributors to tissue degradation, emerging insights from pulp biology emphasize the dynamic interplay between inflammation and regeneration. This interaction involves innate immune responses, inflammatory signaling, and reparative dentinogenesis (Cooper et al. 2010; Farges et al. 2015).

Importantly, dentin is not a passive substrate but a biologically active tissue capable of modulating inflammation and promoting repair. Molecules released from sound dentin, including mineralization-associated proteins and components of the complement system, can stimulate cell migration, differentiation, and mineralization (Okamoto et al. 2018; Pohl et al. 2024; Smith et al. 2012). While these findings suggest that dentin matrix components can elicit reparative processes, it remains unclear whether similar mechanisms are activated during caries progression. As bacteria infiltrate and demineralize dentin, growth factors, cytokines, and matrix proteins are exposed, and endogenous proteases, such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and cathepsins, are activated, contributing to tissue degradation (Tjaderhane et al. 1998; Vidal et al. 2014). Despite these insights, the molecular alterations in carious dentin, particularly across different stages of lesion progression, remain underexplored. A deeper understanding of how the dentin and pulp proteome evolve during caries is essential for elucidating mechanisms of tissue damage and repair.

Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics enables large-scale protein characterization and has been widely applied to dental tissues, especially sound dentin (Park et al. 2009; Salmon et al. 2017; Widbiller et al. 2019). Our recent work comparing sound and carious dentin revealed greater protein diversity in carious tissue (Carrilho et al. 2023). However, proteomic changes across lesion stages remain poorly defined. Caries progression alters the dentin-pulp complex through acidic activation of endogenous enzymes, immune cell infiltration, and microbial invasion, each contributing to matrix degradation and protein release (Ricucci et al. 2017; Tjaderhane et al. 1998; Vidal et al. 2014). Characterizing the dentin proteome across lesion stages can reveal host responses to bacterial invasion and identify stage-specific molecular changes, including dentin matrix proteins, odontoblast-secreted proteins, tertiary dentin components, and proteins derived from pulp or inflammatory cells. These dynamic changes highlight the importance of directly analyzing diseased dentin-pulp complex.

This study explored the proteomic landscape of cavitated caries lesions at advanced, distinct and extensive stages, compared to sound dentin, using MS-based proteomics and bioinformatics. We aimed to identify stage-specific pathways, molecular functions, and regulatory mechanisms involved in caries progression. We hypothesize that the dentin proteome evolves with lesion severity, reflecting host-microbiome interactions and biological changes in the dentin-pulp complex. Recognizing that carious dentin contains proteins from both the matrix and cellular sources (e.g., odontoblasts, immune and pulp cells), our approach captures the dynamic environment of lesion development, including structural breakdown and host responses such as inflammation, remodeling, and defense, offering a comprehensive view of caries progression.

sec.title: Preparation of Dentin Samples and Protein Extraction
sec.p: De-identified human molars with sound or carious dentin were collected under IRB approval (#202310468). Caries lesions were classified as distinct lesions involving the dentin (ICDAS 5) or distinct and extensive lesion involving the dentin (ICDAS 6), and only active, cavitated lesions were included (Appendix Figure 1). Teeth were grouped by dentin condition into six clusters, each containing three teeth with the same classification (n = 6 clusters; total = 18 teeth) (Appendix Figure 2), each yielding approximately 1 g of coronal dentin powder (Comnick 2022). Two sequential protein extracts were obtained per cluster: G1 (pre-demineralization, matrix-unbound) and G2 (post-demineralization, matrix bound). This resulted in six G1 and six G2 extracts across sound (S), distinct dentin caries (DDC), and extensive dentin caries (EDC) groups (Carrilho et al. 2023; Martin-De Las Heras et al. 2000). Detailed protocols are available in the Appendix.

sec.title: Label-free Quantitative Proteomics and Bioinformatics Analyses
sec.p: G1 and G2 protein extracts were reduced, trypsin-digested, and analyzed via label-free LC-MS/MS. Quantification used Minora Feature Detection in Proteome Discoverer (Thermo Scientific), matching spectra to the UniProt Homo sapiens via Mascot and Sequest HT. Downstream analyses in R (v 4.5.1) focused on proteins detected in ≥ 70% of samples (Kong et al. 2022). Statistical analysis using the limma R package applied linear models with empirical Bayes moderated t-tests to compare dentin conditions (S, DDC, and EDC) and extracts (G1 and G2) (Ritchie et al. 2015). Significant differences (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05) were assessed for all comparisons (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA; QIAGEN) identified key pathways, upstream regulators and networks (adjusted p < 0.05). Full methodological details are in the Appendix.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Protein concentrations were similar across G1 and G2 extracts (0.90–1.28 mg/ml), with G2 slightly higher in S and DDC, and lower in EDC (Appendix Table 1). Proteomic profiling identified 320 proteins, with 80 differentially expressed (DE) in EDC×S, 16 in EDC×DDC, and 3 in DDC×S (adjusted p < 0.05). Summary statistics of protein identification are provided in Appendix Table 2. Because G2 and G1 are paired extracts from the same dentin before and after demineralization, results are reported as differential coverage rather than expression, revealing 200 proteins with significant differences (Appendix Table 3). Violin plots (Appendix Figure 3) confirmed data normalization, enabling robust downstream comparative analyses. Principal component analysis showed a clear separation between G1 and G2 profiles, with tighter clustering in G2 (Figure 1A). The full list of proteins with differential recovery in the G2×G1 comparison is reported in Appendix Table 3, and a volcano plot highlights these differences (Figure 1B).

EDC×S revealed 45 downregulated and 35 upregulated proteins (Figure 1C), while EDC×DDC showed 4 downregulated and 12 upregulated proteins (Figure 1D). Only three DE proteins were found in DDC×S—downregulated DSPP and up-regulated S100 and SERPINB1 (Figure 1E), limiting IPA analysis for this comparison. Heatmaps (Figure 2) highlighted DE proteins linked to dental tissues and caries, with consistent upregulation of S100 family members (S100, S100A8, S100A12) and the leukocyte elastase inhibitor (SERPINB1) in EDC. Additional proteins such as azurocidin 1 (AZU1), cystatin SN (CST1), myeloperoxidase (MPO), lactoferrin (LTF), proteinase 3 (PRTN3), ribonuclease 1 (RNASE1), and DSPP showed differential expression predominantly in EDC, with variations between G1 and G2 (Figure 2).

G2 extracts were enriched in proteins associated with dentin formation, mineralization, and structural components of the tissue matrix. These include MMP20, tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 3 (TIMP3), secreted protein acidic and rich in cysteine (SPARC), procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer (PCOLCE), collagen type XI alpha chains (COL11A1, COL11A2), dentin matrix protein 1 (DMP1), collagen triple helix repeat containing 1 (CTHRC1), lysyl oxidase (LOX), extracellular matrix protein 2 (ECM2), dentin sialophosphoprotein (DSPP), secreted phosphoprotein 2 (SPP2), and enamelin (ENAM). Conversely, proteins typically enriched in pulp tissue and involved in immune response, metabolism, or cellular stress—such as glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1), alpha-2-glycoprotein 1 (AZGP1), LTF, hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB), vimentin (VIM), heat shock protein family A member 8 (HSPA8), haptoglobin (HP), MPO, and prolactin-induced protein (PIP)—were downregulated in G2 (Figure 1B, Figure 2B, Appendix Table 3).

Functional enrichment revealed shared processes in EDC, including cell death/survival, growth, maintenance, and free radical scavenging. EDC×S showed unique enrichment in cell signaling, carbohydrate metabolism, and protein synthesis, while EDC×DDC highlighted RNA processing, DNA repair, and cell cycle functions. DDC×S showed fewer enriched functions, including cell signaling, molecular transport, vitamin/mineral metabolism, and cellular development (Figure 3).

Canonical pathway analysis revealed enrichment of immune-related processes, with antimicrobial peptides common across carious comparisons. In EDC×S, highly enriched pathways included altered T and B cell signaling, macrophage alternative activation, autoimmune signaling, and FcγRIIB signaling in B lymphocytes, with top z-scores for neutrophil extracellular traps and antimicrobial peptides (Figure 4A). In contrast, EDC×DDC showed selective enrichment of neutrophil degranulation and autophagy-related pathways, including late endosomal and chaperone-mediated autophagy (Figure 4C). These results indicate overlapping antimicrobial responses alongside distinct immune and stress pathways, with EDC×S showing broader enrichment and stronger network connectivity (Figure 4B) compared to EDC×DDC (Figure 4D). The only canonical pathway enriched in the DDC×S comparison was the HEY1 signaling (graph not shown).

Upstream regulators included IL1A, SERPINB7, BCL3, NFKBIZ, and IL37 in EDC×DDC, and CEBPA in EDC×S. In DDC×S, SERPINB7 and DSPP were linked to IL1RN (interleukin-1 receptor antagonist) and CHI3L1 (chitinase-3-like protein 1) (Appendix Tables 4, 5, and 6). Network analysis revealed four clusters in EDC×S, with two dominant networks (scores 32–58) involving 16–25 molecules linked to inflammation, immune activation, and tissue injury. EDC×DDC had one network (score 30) with 11 molecules including IL6, NF-κB, TLR5, and CRP, consistent with a coordinated innate immune response involving leukocyte signaling and host defense. DDC×S had three low-score networks with minimal connectivity (Figure 5, Appendix Tables 7, 8, and 9).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study presents the first comprehensive proteomic analysis of carious tissues, characterizing protein profile changes across the advanced lesions in comparison to sound dentin. Unlike prior studies that grouped carious dentin from lesions of varying stages (Carrilho et al. 2023), our approach focused on distinct and cavitated lesions involving the dentin considered advanced and extensive (ICDAS 5 and 6), enabling a more precise characterization of molecular changes within the dentin-pulp complex during late disease progression. Our findings reveal that the proteome of carious lesions reflects contributions from multiple sources: the dentin matrix, inflamed pulp tissue, and protein from odontoblasts and immune cells transported via dentinal tubules. Notably, salivary proteins were also detected as we used cavitated lesions. These findings suggest that localized lesions can capture broader cellular responses to caries. Differentially expressed proteins in the EDC×S and EDC×DDC comparisons highlight progressive biological activity in the dentin-pulp complex, consistent with our hypothesis of evolving changes in dentin-pulp complex degradation and remodeling during caries progression.

Proteomic studies of mineralized tissues face inherent technical challenges, making methodological rigor essential for cross-study comparisons. We employed a guanidine-based extraction protocol with sequential EDTA demineralization (Martin-De Las Heras et al. 2000). Although more time-intensive than simpler methods (Park et al. 2009), this approach yielded a robust and comprehensive protein profile, identifying over 300 proteins. These findings align with our recent work demonstrating the value of thorough demineralization for proteomic recovery and highlighting the importance of extract-specific profiling through distinct protein sets in G1 and G2 fractions (Carrilho et al. 2023). Proteins such as DSPP, TIMP3, MMP20, DMP1, COL11A1, COL11A2, TGFB1, VTN, and PCOLCE were consistently abundant in G2 extracts across all dentin conditions. These proteins, many of which are primarily structural extracellular matrix proteins, are known to play key roles in dentin formation, mineralization, and remodeling (Chen et al. 2022), and were mainly extracted following demineralization, indicating their tight association with the mineralized matrix. In contrast, proteins more abundant in the G1 extract, such as RNASE3, MPO, PRTN3, and various immunoglobulins (Figure 2, Appendix Table 3), are likely loosely associated with the tissue, not embedded within the mineralized matrix. Their elevated recovery in G1 extracts from EDC samples suggests they may originate from infiltrating immune cells or salivary components, consistent with the demineralized and inflamed nature of the dentin-pulp complex in these lesions.

It is also important to note that many proteomic studies of dentin rely on limited sample sizes (Carrilho et al. 2023; Park et al. 2009), or use pooled dentin from multiple teeth combined for protein removal (Widbiller et al. 2019). Pooling introduces limitations that can affect protein correlations and functional associations. Additionally, specific biological differences may be lost when dentin is pooled from a relatively large number of teeth (Widbiller et al. 2019). Nevertheless, we adopted a clustering strategy previously validated by our group (Comnick 2022) to ensure methodological rigor, reproducibility, and to account for biological variability. Despite these efforts, sample variability persisted, likely due to the use of de-identified teeth without stratification by donor age, sex, or pulp vitality (although teeth with pulp exposure were excluded). Future studies should aim to mitigate this limitation by incorporating tighter control over donor variables. Nonetheless, the current findings provide valuable initial insights into molecular alterations associated with caries progression. Our findings are consistent with recent studies using pooled permanent and deciduous teeth, which also reported intra-group consistency despite inherent sample variation (Giovani et al. 2021). These patterns are mirrored in our principal component analysis (Figure 1A), supporting the biological relevance of the observed proteomic shifts. To further ensure robustness, we applied an inclusion criterion that retained proteins present in at least 70% of samples (Kong et al. 2022). This threshold allowed us to capture proteins that may vary due to caries lesion severity, anatomical location, and individual biological responses, while minimizing the risk of over-filtering. It also ensured that proteins present in both G1 and G2 extracts were included in comparisons across different tissue conditions. Moreover, the variation in peptide counts and sequence coverage reported herein (Appendix Table 2) aligns with previous studies, which showed peptide counts from 2 to 31 and coverage percentages from 4% to 88% (Eckhardt et al. 2014) and from 0.4% to 51.7% (Park et al. 2009). Looking ahead, incorporating tooth-level identifiers could help account for donor-specific variability in proteomic profiles, influenced by age, systemic health, or clinical history. Linking these profiles to clinical findings and pulp diagnoses would enhance the biological relevance of the data. Additionally, applying even more strict thresholds, such as higher fold-change cutoffs or more rigorous filtering criteria, could help refine the identification of biologically meaningful proteomic changes and reduce noise from low-abundance or inconsistently detected proteins.

Comparative profiling across sound and carious dentin reveals a complex interplay of innate immunity, inflammation, and tissue repair in response to bacterial invasion (Cooper et al. 2010). In sound dentin, enriched molecular and cellular functions suggest regulation of homeostasis, structural integrity, and adaptive responses (Figure 3). Notably, IL1RN—a cytokine receptor antagonist with anti-inflammatory roles in the dentin-pulp complex—is identified as an upstream regulator (Appendix Table 6) (Tazawa et al. 2022). Enriched molecular and cellular functions, such as cell death and survival, cell-to-cell signaling and interaction, and free radical scavenging (Figure 3) reflect the dysregulated physiological responses to infection. Enrichment of antimicrobial peptides, neutrophil degranulation, extracellular trap signaling, and communication between innate and adaptive immune cells (Figure 4) further illustrate the dual nature of tissue destruction and repair. Up-regulated proteins including S100A8, S100A12, PRTN3, DEFA1, LTF, MPO, and AZU1 align with previous studies on immune and inflammatory responses in caries and pulpitis (Figure 2). These proteins are primarily localized in the extracellular space or cytoplasm and are involved in innate immune defense and inflammatory signaling.

As reviewed by Farges et al. (2015) and Pohl et al. (2024), pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) activate Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in odontoblasts, macrophages, dendritic cells, and fibroblasts, triggering antimicrobial agents and proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines to recruit and activate immune and inflammatory cells. Neutrophils, in particular, play a central role in pulpitis through degranulation and production of extracellular trap formation (Pohl et al. 2024), functions enriched in our dataset (Figure 4). S100A8 and S100A9, secreted by neutrophils and macrophages in response to bacterial infection, modulate inflammation via cytokine induction and oxidative stress (Wang et al. 2018). Elevated levels of S100A8 have been reported in carious dentin and inflamed pulp, particularly in symptomatic irreversible pulpitis and advanced caries lesions (Jungbluth et al. 2023; McLachlan et al. 2004; Wang et al. 2023). S100A8 also contributes to bacterial defense through metal chelation and amplifies inflammation via TLR-4 activation and NF-ᴋB signaling (Singh and Ali 2022). Similarly, LTF restricts bacterial growth via metal chelation or sequestration (Gruden and Poklar Ulrih 2021; Jaberi et al. 2021), while PRTN3, a neutrophil serine protease, is involved in bacterial membrane disruption (Korkmaz et al. 2010). DEFA1, a small antimicrobial peptide is also neutrophil-derived and has been linked to increased caries risk when salivary levels are low (Ozsin-Ozler et al. 2022). Some of these proteins show upregulation and predicted activation in specific cellular compartments including LTF and HBB in the extracellular space, PRTN3 in the plasma, S100A8 and S100A12 in the cytoplasm, and NK-ᴋB complex in the nucleus, as shown in the interaction network for EDC×DDC (Figure 5). Together, these findings highlight a coordinated immune response within the dentin-pulp complex, where the balance between microbial defense and inflammation plays a critical role in shaping the molecular landscape of caries progression.

Persistent bacterial infection drives chronic inflammation, which may represent a shift in the inflammatory mode rather than a distinct response. Our data suggests features of chronic inflammation, including recruitment of T and B cells, supported by enriched canonical pathways in the EDC×S comparison (Figure 3) and up-regulation of RARRES2 (Figure 2, G1 extracts only), a modulator of NK and T cell migration (Pachynski et al. 2019). IL1A and IL17A are shown as an upstream regulators in EDC×DDC comparison (Appendix Table 5) and IL-1β has been reported in the literature as one of the potential key regulators of immune cells in pulpitis (Wang et al. 2023). These results suggest an escalation of inflammatory responses in extensive caries (Cooper et al. 2010; Pohl et al. 2024).

In addition to the immune-related proteins discussed above, fibrinogen subunits (FGA, FGB) and HBB emerged as key targets of upstream regulators in the EDC×DDC comparison (Appendix Table 5; Figure 5). Fibrinogen may limit bacterial invasion and reduce dentin permeability but can also be exploited by bacteria via the plasminogen/plasmin pathway to degrade the extracellular matrix (Love 2002; Yatsenko et al. 2023). Hemoglobin and its fragments activate TLRs and promote oxidative stress, leading to NF-κB activation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, which contribute to tissue damage in irreversible pulpitis (Kokkas et al. 2007; Lee and Ding 2013; McLachlan et al. 2004; Wang et al. 2023).

In conclusion, this study highlights the complexity of protein-level changes and their structural and functional implications in dental caries. The differential regulation of proteins across advanced caries stages reflects a dynamic interplay between extracellular matrix remodeling, intracellular signaling, and immune activation. Importantly, while immune and inflammatory pathways were identified, these likely represent secondary responses to dentin matrix degradation rather than primary drivers of the observed proteomic shifts. While the presence of cellular proteins may limit the ability to attribute findings solely to dentin matrix degradation, they offer valuable insight into the biological processes active at each stage of lesion development. Therefore, we interpret the differences in protein profiles not as isolated markers of dentin structure, but as integrated indicators of the biological environment within advanced carious lesions. Future studies should integrate clinical metadata and apply refined analytical thresholds to further clarify the roles of specific proteins of the dentin-pulp complex in caries disease.

caption.p: A. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of protein abundance in imputed data. The plot shows the distribution of samples along the first two principal components, Dim1 (27% variance) and Dim2 (12% variance), capturing the variation in protein abundance across different sample groups. Each point represents an individual sample, colored according to the protein extract and dentin condition: G1, Sound (red); G2, Sound (yellow); G1, Distinct Dentin Caries (green); G2, Distinct Dentin Caries (blue); G1, Extensive Dentin Caries (purple); and G2, Extensive Dentin Caries (pink). Concentration ellipses (95% probability level) are provided for each group, highlighting group clustering and separation based on protein abundance profiles. B, C, D, E. Volcano plots indicate protein expression data for G2 vs G1 (B), Extensive Dentin Caries vs Sound (C), Extensive Dentin Caries vs Distinct Dentin Caries (D), and Distinct Dentin Caries vs Sound (E) comparisons. The x-axis represents the log2 fold change in protein expression, while the y-axis represents the statistical significance as adjusted p-values (-log10(Adj P value)). Each dot represents a protein, with red indicating significantly upregulated (positive logFC) and blue indicating significantly downregulated proteins (negative logFC). Gray dots represent proteins with non-significant changes in expression (adjusted p-value > 0.05).

Heatmaps illustrating the expression profiles of sets of proteins differentially expressed clustered according to the different dentin conditions (A) and with differential coverage in G2 versus G1 protein extracts (B). Rows correspond to proteins, and columns correspond to specific dentin conditions (EDC = extensive dentin caries, DDC = distinct dentin caries, S = sound dentin) and protein extracts (G2 and G1). The color intensity represents the relative protein expression, with red indicating upregulation compared to the average normalized expression of the protein and blue indicating downregulation. Hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and complete linkage was applied to group proteins with similar expression patterns.

Comparison of molecular and cellular functions based on pathway enrichment analysis. The different sets of enriched molecular functions represent Extensive Dentin Caries vs Sound, Extensive Dentin Caries vs Distinct Dentin Caries, and Distinct Dentin Caries vs Sound ranked by −log(p-value). Each bar corresponds to a specific molecular or cellular process, with longer bars indicating higher statistical significance of enrichment. The yellow line represents the threshold for statistical significance. A −log(p-value) ≥ 1.3 corresponds to a p-value of 0.05. Image was generated using QIAGEN Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA, QIAGEN Inc., www.qiagen.com/ingenuity).

Canonical pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed proteins (A and C) and overlap network of differentially expressed proteins (B and D) for Extensive Dentin Caries vs Sound and Extensive Dentin Caries vs Distinct Dentin Caries. Enriched canonical pathways charts display the enriched pathways according to the −log(p-value). Bars in orange indicate pathways with positive z-score. Bars in white or gray indicate z-score = 0 and no activity pattern available, respectively. The networks illustrate shared regulatory nodes between interactions and overlaps among the enriched pathways. The intense red color nodes indicate pathways with predominantly up-regulated molecules, suggesting increased involvement or activity of those pathways under the analyzed conditions, while pink nodes represent a mix of upregulated and downregulated molecules within the pathway. A −log(p-value) ≥ 1.3 corresponds to a p-value of 0.05. Image was generated using QIAGEN Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA, QIAGEN Inc., www.qiagen.com/ingenuity).

Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA)-generated interaction networks from lists of differentially expressed proteins in the Extensive Dentin Caries vs Sound (EDC×S), Extensive Dentin Caries vs Distinct Dentin Caries (EDC×DDC), and Distinct Dentin Caries vs Sound (DDC×S) comparisons. The top two networks in the EDC×S, the only network in EDC×DDC, and the third network in DDC×S (with more molecules in the network) are shown (see Appendix Tables 7, 8, and 9 for additional information). The prediction legend applies to all networks. Image was generated using QIAGEN Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA, QIAGEN Inc., www.qiagen.com/ingenuity).
